## Overview

HarmonyDream is a simple yet effective approach that automatically adjusts loss coefficients to maintain task harmonization—a dynamic equilibrium between the two tasks in world model learning.

## Problem and Key Insights

Model-based reinforcement learning uses world models that typically encompass two tasks: observation modeling and reward modeling, and the paper uncovers the overlooked potential of sample-efficient MBRL by mitigating the domination of either task.

The key insight is that while explicit MBRL approaches attempt to restore abundant details via observation models (which is difficult due to environment complexity and limited model capacity), reward models are inadequate for sample-efficient learning without richer learning signals.

## Loss Balancing Approach

HarmonyDream dynamically balances the overall loss scales across tasks in world model learning, considering together per-dimension scales, dimensions, and training dynamics. This differs from static approaches like DreamerV3's symlog transformation.

## Results

The base MBRL method equipped with HarmonyDream gains 10%-69% absolute performance boosts on visual robotic tasks and sets a new state-of-the-art result on the Atari 100K benchmark.

The paper was published at the Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning in 2024.

## Overview of SPR

Self-Predictive Representations (SPR) trains an agent to predict its own latent state representations multiple steps into the future. An agent can learn more efficiently if reward maximization is augmented with self-supervised objectives based on structure in its visual input and sequential interaction with the environment.

## Stop-Gradient in SPR

The stop-gradient operation is a critical component of the SPR architecture. Properly regularized SPR avoids trivial solutions (collapse to constant representations), a property provably enforced by the use of stop-gradient and momentum updates for the target networks. SPR in which target representations are generated by the online encoder without a stop-gradient exhibits catastrophically reduced performance.

## Architecture Details

Target representations for future states are computed using an encoder which is an exponential moving average of the agent's parameters and predictions are made using a learned transition model. The target encoder, maintained via exponential moving average (EMA) update of online parameters, generates targets for self-prediction while being frozen with respect to the current gradient computation.

## Empirical Results

The full self-supervised objective, which combines future prediction and data augmentation, achieves a median human-normalized score of 0.415 on Atari in a setting limited to 100k steps of environment interaction, which represents a 55% relative improvement over the previous state-of-the-art.

## Overview

VICReg (Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization) was authored by Adrien Bardes, Jean Ponce, and Yann LeCun, with the paper submitted on May 11, 2021 and last revised on January 28, 2022. The work was published at ICLR 2022.

## Key Contribution

VICReg introduces a method that explicitly avoids the collapse problem with a simple regularization term on the variance of the embeddings along each dimension individually. The method uses two regularization terms applied to both embeddings separately: (1) a term that maintains the variance of each embedding dimension above a threshold, (2) a term that decorrelates each pair of variables.

## Technical Approach

VICReg combines the variance term with a decorrelation mechanism based on redundancy reduction and covariance regularization, and achieves results on par with the state of the art on several downstream tasks. 

Unlike most other approaches to the same problem, VICReg does not require techniques such as: weight sharing between the branches, batch normalization, feature-wise normalization, output quantization, stop gradient, memory banks, etc.

## Official Resources

Meta AI and Inria provide a PyTorch implementation and pretrained models for VICReg, with the official repository available on GitHub (facebookresearch/vicreg).

## Overview

BYOL-Explore is a conceptually simple yet general approach for curiosity-driven exploration in visually complex environments. The strategy is based on Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL), a self-supervised latent-predictive method that forecasts an earlier version of its latent representation.

## How It Works

BYOL-Explore learns a world representation, the world dynamics, and an exploration policy all-together by optimizing a single prediction loss in the latent space with no additional auxiliary objective. BYOL-Explore learns a world model with a self-supervised prediction loss and trains a curiosity-driven policy using the same loss.

## Key Innovation

While previous works focused primarily on using the world-model for representation learning in RL, BYOL-Explore takes this one step further, and not only learns a versatile world model but also uses the world model's loss to drive exploration.

## Performance

BYOL-Explore is effective in DM-HARD-8, a challenging partially-observable continuous-action hard-exploration benchmark with visually-rich 3-D environments. On this benchmark, it solves the majority of the tasks purely through augmenting the extrinsic reward with BYOL-Explore's intrinsic reward, whereas prior work could only get off the ground with human demonstrations. It also achieves superhuman performance on the ten hardest exploration games in Atari while having a much simpler design than other competitive agents.

## The Dormant Neuron Phenomenon in Deep Reinforcement Learning by Sokar et al. (2023)

The research identifies the dormant neuron phenomenon in deep reinforcement learning, where an agent's network suffers from an increasing number of inactive neurons, thereby affecting network expressivity.

**Key Findings:**

The phenomenon is demonstrated across a variety of algorithms and environments, highlighting its effect on learning. The number of dormant neurons increases as training progresses, and while agents start training with a small number of dormant neurons, this number increases as training progresses. Notably, this is in contrast with supervised learning, where the number of dormant neurons remains low throughout training.

**Proposed Solution:**

The researchers propose a simple and effective method called ReDo (Recycling Dormant neurons) that maintains the expressive power of networks by reducing the number of dormant neurons and results in improved performance.

**Publication Details:**

## TD-MPC: Temporal Difference Learning for Model Predictive Control

The paper "Temporal Difference Learning for Model Predictive Control" was published at ICML 2022 by authors Nicklas Hansen, Xiaolong Wang, and Hao Su.

### Overview

The method uses a learned task-oriented latent dynamics model for local trajectory optimization over a short horizon, and a learned terminal value function to estimate long-term return, both learned jointly by temporal difference learning.

### Key Contributions

TD-MPC achieves superior sample efficiency and asymptotic performance over prior work on both state and image-based continuous control tasks from DMControl and Meta-World. The method solves high-dimensional Humanoid and Dog locomotion tasks in 1M environment steps and is, to the best of their knowledge, the first documented result solving the challenging Dog tasks.

### Technical Approach

TD-MPC is a framework for MPC using a Task-Oriented Latent Dynamics (TOLD) model and terminal value function, both learned jointly by temporal difference learning. During inference, trajectory optimization is performed with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control over latent model rollouts with the value function for long-term return estimates.

The code and additional resources are available at https://nicklashansen.github.io/td-mpc.

## Paper Overview

The paper "Maxmin Q-learning: Controlling the Estimation Bias of Q-learning" was authored by Qingfeng Lan, Yangchen Pan, Alona Fyshe, and Martha White, and it was published at the 8th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2020).

## Main Contribution

Maxmin Q-learning directly mitigates the overestimation bias by using a minimization over multiple action-value estimates. Moreover, it is able to control the estimation bias varying from positive to negative which helps improve learning efficiency.

## Key Insights

Q-learning suffers from overestimation bias, because it approximates the maximum action value using the maximum estimated action value. Algorithms have been proposed to reduce overestimation bias, but there was a lack of understanding of how bias interacts with performance, and the extent to which existing algorithms mitigate bias.

The paper showed theoretically that estimation bias and estimation variance can be decreased by choosing an appropriate number N of action-value functions.

## Overview

Standard deep-learning methods gradually lose plasticity in continual-learning settings until they learn no better than a shallow network. Loss of plasticity is a phenomenon where networks may lose their ability to learn on new examples.

## The Continual Backpropagation Algorithm

Plasticity is maintained indefinitely only by algorithms that continually inject diversity into the network, such as continual backpropagation, a variation of backpropagation in which a small fraction of less-used units are continually and randomly reinitialized.

## Key Findings

Methods based on gradient descent are not enough—sustained deep learning requires a random, non-gradient component to maintain variability and plasticity. In ImageNet, binary classification performance dropped from 89% accuracy on an early task down to 77%, about the level of a linear network, on the 2000th task.

## Publication

The research was published in Nature, volume 632, pages 768-774, in 2024, authored by Dohare, Hernandez-Garcia, Lan, Rahman, Mahmood, and Sutton.

The work has generated significant follow-up research, with other groups exploring refinements to the continual backpropagation approach and alternative strategies for maintaining plasticity in neural networks.

## Overview

Plasticity, the ability of a neural network to quickly change its predictions in response to new information, is essential for the adaptability and robustness of deep reinforcement learning systems.

## Main Findings

Deep neural networks are known to lose plasticity over the course of training even in relatively simple learning problems, but the mechanisms driving this phenomenon are still poorly understood. This paper conducts a systematic empirical analysis into plasticity loss, with the goal of understanding the phenomenon mechanistically in order to guide the future development of targeted solutions.

The key discovery is that loss of plasticity is deeply connected to changes in the curvature of the loss landscape, but that it often occurs in the absence of saturated units.

## Solutions Proposed

Based on this insight, the authors identify a number of parameterization and optimization design choices which enable networks to better preserve plasticity over the course of training.

## Publication

The paper was published in the Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2023), Honolulu, Hawaii. The authors are Clare Lyle, Zeyu Zheng, Evgenii Nikishin, Bernardo Avila Pires, Razvan Pascanu, and Will Dabney.

DreamerPro is a reconstruction-free MBRL agent that can enhance robustness to distractions. Motivated by the recent success of prototypical representations, a non-contrastive self-supervised learning approach in computer vision, DreamerPro combines Dreamer with prototypes.

In order for the prototypes to benefit temporal dynamics learning in MBRL, the authors propose to additionally learn the prototypes from the recurrent states of the world model, thereby distilling temporal structures from past observations and actions into the prototypes.

## Overview
Time-Aware World Model (TAWM) is a model-agnostic and more efficient training method for world models, presented by Anh N. Nhu, Sanghyun Son, and Ming C. Lin from University of Maryland, College Park at ICML 2025.

## Core Contribution
TAWM is a model-based approach that explicitly incorporates temporal dynamics. By conditioning on the time-step size rather than sampling at a fixed time-step, TAWM learns both high- and low-frequency task dynamics across diverse control problems.

## Key Insight
Grounded in the information-theoretic insight that the optimal sampling rate depends on a system's underlying dynamics, this time-aware formulation improves both performance and data efficiency.

## Performance
TAWM consistently outperforms conventional models across varying observation rates in a variety of control tasks, using the same number of training samples and iterations.

## Architecture
While TAWM is built on top of TD-MPC2 world model architecture as the basis of the experiments, its core contribution is the time-aware training method, which is architecture-agnostic and can be incorporated into any world model training pipeline.

## Resources
The official code is available at github.com/anh-nn01/Time-Aware-World-Model, with the paper published in the Forty-second International Conference on Machine Learning (2025).

## Overview

PCGrad is a method called Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) to improve the optimization challenges of multi-task learning. The approach projects a task's gradient onto the normal plane of the gradient of any other task that has a conflicting gradient, and leads to substantial gains in efficiency and performance on multi-task supervised and multi-task RL problems.

## The Problem: The "Tragic Triad"

The key challenges are when task gradients conflict (point in opposite directions), occur in areas of high curvature, and have large differences in magnitude. Two gradients are defined as conflicting if they point away from one another, i.e., have a negative cosine similarity.

## How PCGrad Works

PCGrad determines whether task gradients conflict by computing the cosine similarity between vectors, where negative values indicate conflicting gradients. If the cosine similarity is negative, it replaces the gradient by its projection onto the normal plane of the other gradient, and if gradients are not in conflict, the original gradient remains unaltered.

## Key Strengths

It is model-agnostic and can be combined with previously-proposed multi-task architectures for enhanced performance. PCGrad leads to substantially better data efficiency, optimization speed, and performance compared to prior methods in multi-task classification, scene understanding, reinforcement learning, and goal-conditioned RL.

## "Deep Reinforcement Learning with Plasticity Injection" - Nikishin et al., NeurIPS 2023

The paper introduces plasticity injection, a minimalistic intervention that increases network plasticity without changing the number of trainable parameters or biasing predictions.

### Key Motivation
A growing body of evidence suggests that neural networks employed in deep reinforcement learning (RL) gradually lose their plasticity—the ability to learn from new data.

### Main Applications
The paper has two primary applications:

1. **Diagnostic Tool**: If injection increases performance, one can conclude that an agent's network was losing its plasticity, allowing identification of a subset of Atari environments where the lack of plasticity causes performance plateaus.

2. **Computational Efficiency**: Plasticity injection can improve the computational efficiency of RL training if the agent has to re-learn from scratch due to exhausted plasticity or by growing the agent's network dynamically without compromising performance.

### Results
The results on Atari show that plasticity injection attains stronger performance compared to alternative methods while being computationally efficient.

**Authors**: Evgenii Nikishin, Junhyuk Oh, Georg Ostrovski, Clare Lyle, Razvan Pascanu, Will Dabney, and André Barreto.

## COMBO: Conservative Offline Model-Based Policy Optimization

COMBO is a model-based reinforcement learning algorithm that learns a dynamics model from logged experience and performs conservative planning under the learned model as a promising paradigm for offline reinforcement learning.

### Key Innovation

COMBO regularizes the value function on out-of-support state-action tuples generated via rollouts under the learned model. This results in a conservative estimate of the value function for out-of-support state-action tuples, without requiring explicit uncertainty estimation.

### Problem It Addresses

Practical variants of model-based algorithms rely on explicit uncertainty quantification for incorporating conservatism, but uncertainty estimation with complex models such as deep neural networks can be difficult and unreliable, and empirically leads to poor performance in certain scenarios in offline model-based RL.

### Theoretical Guarantees

The method theoretically optimizes a lower bound on the true policy value, with a bound that is tighter than that of prior methods, and satisfies a policy improvement guarantee in the offline setting.

### Performance

Through experiments, COMBO consistently performs as well or better as compared to prior offline model-free and model-based methods on widely studied offline RL benchmarks, including image-based tasks.

The paper was initially submitted in February 2021 and updated in January 2022, making it a significant contribution to the offline reinforcement learning literature around that time period.

## VaGraM: Value Gradient weighted Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (ICLR 2022)

VaGraM is a Value-Gradient weighted Model loss that rescales the mean squared error loss function with gradient information from the current value function estimate.

### Key Concept
The key insight is to include the value function into the loss as a measure of the sensitivity of model errors for different data points and observation dimensions, by computing a convex approximation of the value function around each data point through its first order Taylor approximation (squared), giving a measure of how sensitive the value function is to distortions in the state space.

### Motivation
The theory underlying VaGraM tells us that a value-aligned loss function should matter most in scenarios where the model is insufficient to capture the full complexity of the environment, or in cases where there are irrelevant dimensions in the state space for the control task.

### Experimental Results

## Overview

DisCor is a paper titled "Corrective Feedback in Reinforcement Learning via Distribution Correction" by Aviral Kumar and 2 other authors, and was published on March 16, 2020.

## Core Problem

Deep reinforcement learning can learn effective policies for a wide range of tasks, but is notoriously difficult to use due to instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters. The reasons for this remain unclear. The paper studies how RL methods based on bootstrapping-based Q-learning can suffer from a pathological interaction between function approximation and the data distribution used to train the Q-function: with standard supervised learning, online data collection should induce corrective feedback, where new data corrects mistakes in old predictions. With dynamic programming methods like Q-learning, such feedback may be absent.

The authors propose a new algorithm, DisCor, which explicitly optimizes for data distributions that can correct for accumulated errors in the value function. DisCor computes a tractable approximation to the distribution that optimally induces corrective feedback, which results in reweighting samples based on the estimated accuracy of their target values.

## Results and Applications

Using this distribution for training, DisCor results in substantial improvements in a range of challenging RL settings, such as multi-task learning and learning from noisy reward signals. The paper was published as part of Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020).

## Overview

The work identifies a common flaw of deep reinforcement learning algorithms: a tendency to rely on early interactions and ignore useful evidence encountered later. Because of training on progressively growing datasets, deep RL agents incur a risk of overfitting to earlier experiences, negatively affecting the rest of the learning process.

## Key Finding and Solution

This effect is referred to as the primacy bias, inspired by cognitive science. Through a series of experiments, the authors dissect the algorithmic aspects of deep RL that exacerbate this bias.

The solution proposed is elegant: The authors propose to freely increase the replay ratio, but periodically perform a weight reset to reinitialize all of the agent's weights while preserving the replay buffer.

## Applications and Impact

The mechanism is applied to algorithms in both discrete (Atari 100k) and continuous action (DeepMind Control Suite) domains, consistently improving their performance. The approach has proven influential—subsequent work has adapted and built upon the reset strategy by completely resetting all agent parameters every 2.56 × 10^6 of its updates.

## Problem Statement and Solution

While model-free reinforcement learning is powerful, its sample efficiency is often impractically large for real-world problems, and the learning signal consists only of scalar rewards, ignoring much of the information in state transitions. TDMs combine the benefits of model-free and model-based RL by leveraging the rich information in state transitions to learn efficiently while attaining asymptotic performance that exceeds direct model-based methods.
